verses.text: The queen of Sheba heard about how famous Solomon was because of the name of the LORD. So she came to test him with hard questions.

She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large group of servants and camels carrying spices, a great amount of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about everything she had on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. Nothing was too hard for the king to explain to her.
The queen of Sheba saw how wise Solomon was. She saw the palace he had built,
the food on his table, the seating of his officials, his servants in their uniforms, his cup-bearers, and the burnt offerings he made at the LORD's temple. It took her breath away.
She said to the king, "Everything I heard in my own country about your achievements and your wisdom is true.
But I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes. And I was not told even half of it! Your wisdom and wealth are much greater than what I heard.
How happy your people must be! How happy are these officials who always stand before you and listen to your wisdom!

Praise the LORD your God! He was pleased with you and put you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD's love for Israel lasts forever, he has made you king, so that you can do what is fair and right."

Then she gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, about four thousand kilograms, a very large amount of spices, and precious stones. Never again did anyone bring as many spices as the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
Hiram's ships, which brought gold from Ophir, also brought large amounts of almug wood and precious stones from Ophir.

The king used the almug wood to make railings for the LORD's temple and for the royal palace, and to make harps and lyres for the musicians. No such almug wood has ever been brought in or seen since that day.

King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she wanted and asked for, besides all the gifts he had already given her out of his royal riches. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
Every year Solomon received six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, about twenty-three thousand kilograms.
This did not include the money from traders and merchants, and from all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold. Each shield used six hundred shekels of gold, about seven kilograms.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold. Each used three minas of gold, almost two kilograms. The king put them in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon.
Then the king made a large throne of ivory and covered it with the finest gold.
The throne had six steps, and its back had a rounded top. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. Nothing like it had ever been made in any other kingdom.

All of King Solomon's drinking cups were made of gold, and all the dishes in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon were made of pure gold. Nothing was made of silver, because silver was thought to be of little value in Solomon's time.
The king had a fleet of trading ships at sea, together with Hiram's ships. Once every three years the ships came back carrying gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon was greater in riches and wisdom than all the other kings of the earth.
People from all over the world wanted to visit Solomon to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Year after year, everyone who came brought a gift: things made of silver and gold, clothes, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon gathered chariots and horses. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He kept some in the chariot cities and some with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as common as the fig trees in the western hills.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt. The king's traders bought them in herds, each herd at a set price.
A chariot from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse cost one hundred and fifty shekels. The traders also sold them to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
